power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

ownership.dep_title: EpiNow2: Estimate and Forecast Real-Time Infection Dynamics
ownership.dep_description: Estimates the time-varying reproduction number, rate of spread, and doubling time using a renewal equation approach combined with Bayesian inference via Stan. Supports Gaussian process and random walk priors for modelling changes in transmission over time. Accounts for delays between infection and observation (incubation period, reporting delays), right-truncation in recent data, day-of-week effects, and observation overdispersion. Can estimate relationships between primary and secondary outcomes (e.g., cases to hospitalisations or deaths) and forecast both. Runs across multiple regions in parallel. Based on Abbott et al. (2020) and Gostic et al. (2020) .

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 2 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

#### Execution
**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 79 scripts: 11 ran without error, 45 errored, 0 timed out, 10 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 1 did not parse, and 11 were run by another script with `source()`. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. **1 script needs the internet**, which is off during the run: get_humidity.R. Keeping what they download in the deposit solves this. **4 scripts use an object or function that only another script defines**, so in the second run that script was loaded first, in the same session: `plot_all_holidays.R` after `holidays.R`; `plot_eval_acefa.R` after `common.R`; `plot_model_comparison.R` after `common.R`; `perf_lp.R` after `common.R`. text.text: Respiratory viruses impose a substantial burden of morbidity and mortality globally, and models that forecast this burden are widely used to support public health decision-making.
However, the public health utility of these forecasts can be limited by poor predictive accuracy.
In this work, we show how capturing the effects of school holidays, public holidays and seasonal changes in transmission can improve respiratory virus forecasting performance.

We construct a Bayesian renewal model where the effective reproduction number R(t ) is composed of log-additive components including school and public holiday effects and an annually-periodic Gaussian process.
The model also allows for the relative rate of reporting to vary with school and public holidays.
We use this model to forecast respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), influenza and SARS-CoV-2 case incidence across a 28-day horizon over five jurisdictions in Australia.
Applied to the 2025 winter season, our forecasts outperform a random-walk baseline forecast across all settings.
We find that the inclusion of holiday and seasonal transmission effects improved forecasting performance across the three pathogens.
We show that the school holidays are associated with populationwide reductions in R(t ) on the order of 5-15% but are generally not associated with changes in reporting.
Collectively, our results provide support for the inclusion of holiday and seasonal effects in future respiratory virus forecasting models.

The global health burden of respiratory viruses is substantial, with influenza virus and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) alone estimated to lead to millions of hospitalisations and hundreds of thousands of deaths every year (Iuliano et al. 2018; Savic et al. 2023; Mazur et al. 2024; Hanage and Schaffner 2025).

text.text: Forecasts can provide intelligence to support public health decision-makers as they prepare for and respond to epidemics of respiratory viruses (Muscatello et al. 2017; Johnson et al. 2022; Christen et al. 2026), and a range of forecasting programs have been launched internationally to produce and share such forecasts (Henderson et al. 2026; Gozzi et al. 2026; Hines et al. 2026; MacArthur et al. 2026).

text.text: Despite substantial advances made in the field over the past decade, improving the performance of respiratory virus forecasts remains an active area of research.

The dynamics of seasonal respiratory virus transmission are the product of complex interactions between patterns in human behaviour, viral transmissibility changes, the build-up and loss of immunity, and demographic turnover (Altizer et al. 2006; Eggo 1 . et al. 2016; Bents et al. 2026; Rubin et al. 2026; Tobin et al. 2026).

text.text: Despite these complexities, patterns in how case incidence data changes over time are still able to be identified, and capturing these patterns within forecasting models provides an opportunity for the improvement of forecast performance.

For example, it is regularly observed that, in temperate regions, the incidence of many respiratory viruses is greatest in wintertime and lowest in summertime (Altizer et al. 2006; Moriyama et al. 2020; Kronfeld-Schor et al. 2021).

text.text: In this work, we develop a Bayesian renewal model to forecast respiratory virus case incidence.

Our model captures the effects of school holidays, public holidays and seasonal changes in transmission upon the effective reproduction number R(t ), as well as the effects of school and public holidays upon the relative rate of case reporting.
We apply the model to retrospectively forecast daily RSV, influenza and SARS-CoV-2 case incidence across the 2025 epidemic season in five Australian jurisdictions over a fourweek time horizon.
We evaluate performance and examine how this performance is affected by the inclusion of different model components.

Using the model fit from the final round of forecasts (which utilises the most complete dataset), we examine the estimated transmission and reporting effects, including the effect of school holidays and season on R(t ).

Our forecasting model estimates the effective reproduction number R(t ) by decomposing the quantity log-additively into school and public holiday effects, an annuallyperiodic seasonal Gaussian process, and a non-periodic noise Gaussian process (Figure 1A).
text.formatted: Our forecasting model estimates the effective reproduction number R(t ) by decomposing the quantity log-additively into school and public holiday effects, an annuallyperiodic seasonal Gaussian process, and a non-periodic noise Gaussian process (Figure <ref type="figure">1A</ref>).

text.text: We relate this R(t ) to infection incidence through a renewal process (Cori et al. 2013; Abbott et al. 2020), and infection incidence to case incidence via a delay convolution.
text.formatted: We relate this R(t ) to infection incidence through a renewal process <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Cori et al. 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Abbott et al. 2020)</ref>, and infection incidence to case incidence via a delay convolution.

text.text: This case incidence may then further be modified by school and public holiday reporting effects.
To produce forecasts, we project R(t ) ahead 28 days, and from this simulate future infection incidence and case incidence.
A full description of the model is provided in the Methods.

To illustrate this approach, we present a forecast that was produced across influenza data from Victoria at a time of increasing case incidence, with school holidays occurring during the forecast horizon (Figure 1).

text.text: In this example, the combined effect of the seasonal Gaussian process and the estimated school holiday transmission effect yields a projected reduction in R(t ) to below one in the immediate horizon of the forecast, and we therefore project a peak in case incidence.
The case incidence that was eventually observed falls largely within the central 50% credible intervals predicted.

While we estimated no substantial effect of the school holidays upon reporting here, the effect of the King's Birthday public holiday on the 9th of June is visible (with approximately a halving in the relative rate of reporting).

We produced 28-day-ahead forecasts of RSV, influenza and SARS-CoV-2 daily case incidence across five jurisdictions in Australia, with a total of 510 forecasts retrospectively produced across the 2025 epidemic season (approx.
February-December).
The five jurisdictions were selected to capture a range of epidemiological settings (with typical seasons in each exhibiting distinct transmission dynamics, Supplementary Figures 2 3 4).

text.text: Performance was assessed using the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) across log-transformed counts.

Forecasting performance was generally best in the jurisdictions with larger population sizes of New South Wales (NSW, 8.6M residents), Queensland (QLD, 5.7M residents) and Victoria (VIC, 7.1M residents), while performance in the Australian Capital Territory (ACT, 0.5M residents) and the Northern Territory (NT, 0.3M residents) was generally poorer (Figure 2A, Australian Bureau of Statistics 2025).

The effect of the seasonal Gaussian process f seasonal (t ) on R(t ) was of the largest magnitude for RSV, where we observed annual increases and decreases of around 20-25% for all jurisdictions except the Northern Territory (Figure 5C).

text.text: The effect grew earliest in the year for the jurisdictions with sub-tropical population centres of New South Wales and Queensland, while increases began later in the year for the temperate jurisdictions of Victoria and the Australian Capital Territory.

The effects of f seasonal (t ) for influenza were of lower amplitude, with increases and decreases on the order of 5-10%, which is comparable to the amplitude of the noise Gaussian process term f noise (t ) in all jurisdictions.
The effect of f seasonal (t ) was found to be the least substantive for SARS-CoV-2, although a small increase in R(t ) of around 5% around April was consistently identified across jurisdictions.

We have presented a Bayesian respiratory virus forecasting model where we capture recurring variation in the effective reproduction number R(t ) through school and public holiday effects and an annually-periodic seasonal Gaussian process.
Our model further captures recurring changes in the relative rate of reporting that may arise across school and public holidays.
We have shown that our model exhibits excellent forecasting performance in contexts where these effects are predictive of epidemic dynamics.
This predictive capability was most evident in forecasts of RSV and in the jurisdictions within Australia with larger population sizes.

Even for pathogens where our model was not able to capture the primary drivers of epidemic growth (e.g. the emergence of new antigenic variants of influenza or SARS-CoV-2), performance was best overall where both holiday and seasonal effects were included in the model.

We also estimated the effects of holidays on respiratory virus dynamics and found the strongest effects to be those of the between-term school holidays on R(t ) and of the public holidays on the relative rate of reporting.

Across the five jurisdictions in Australia and the three respiratory viruses we considered in this work, we found that the school holidays were often associated with changes in transmission but less so with changes in reporting.
The transmission effects that we estimated -on the order of a 5-15% reduction in R(t ) -are consistent with prior work.

For example, Ewing et al. (2017) estimated that the R(t ) of influenza-like-illness reduced by approximately 15% across the winter holidays in the US, while Wang et al. (2026) estimated a 14% reduction in the R(t ) of influenza A(H1N1) across the 2009 summer holidays in China.

(2026)</ref> estimated a 14% reduction in the R(t ) of influenza A(H1N1) across the 2009 summer holidays in China.

text.text: Our population-level estimates are naturally lower than age-specific estimates of reductions in transmission between children during the school holidays, which have been reported to be on the order of 25-45% (Cauchemez et al. 2008; Eggo et al. 2016).

text.text: Our estimates are valuable in informing our understanding of respiratory virus dynamics, as even small recurring changes in transmission can have an outsized effect on quantities such as final size, peak size and peak timing (Altizer et al. 2006; Eames 2014; Tobin et al. 2026).

text.text: Our finding that public holidays have substantial effects on reporting aligns with prior research internationally that has found substantial changes in the rate of testing and reporting across public holidays (Lee et al. 2023; Rumack 2023).
text.formatted: Our finding that public holidays have substantial effects on reporting aligns with prior research internationally that has found substantial changes in the rate of testing and reporting across public holidays <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Lee et al. 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Rumack 2023)</ref>.

text.text: While it has been previously reported that public holidays can lead to reductions in contact rates between individuals (Van Hoang et al. 2021; Son et al. 2025), we did not find convincing evidence of any corresponding change in the rate of transmission.
text.formatted: While it has been previously reported that public holidays can lead to reductions in contact rates between individuals (Van <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Hoang et al. 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Son et al. 2025)</ref>, we did not find convincing evidence of any corresponding change in the rate of transmission.

text.text: However, such changes may be difficult to infer from case incidence data alone, as delays between infection and reporting are likely to obscure the effect of a single-day change in transmission.

Incorporation of public holiday effects in operational forecasting models may be better achieved through use of additional data streams such as ongoing, frequent contact surveys (Golding et al. 2023).
text.formatted: Incorporation of public holiday effects in operational forecasting models may be better achieved through use of additional data streams such as ongoing, frequent contact surveys <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Golding et al. 2023)</ref>.

text.text: While the inclusion of all holiday effects in our model improved forecasting performance, we found that the impact was more mixed when broken down by type of holiday or type of effect.

For example, the inclusion of the school holiday transmission and reporting effects resulted in improved forecasting performance for SARS-CoV-2 and influenza but not RSV, where performance was marginally worse.

This difference may be a consequence of RSV cases most often occurring in children younger than school-age (Mazur et al. 2024), so the school holidays presumably impact a smaller fraction of potential transmission events.
text.formatted: This difference may be a consequence of RSV cases most often occurring in children younger than school-age <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Mazur et al. 2024)</ref>, so the school holidays presumably impact a smaller fraction of potential transmission events.

text.text: The seasonal Gaussian process component of the forecasting model proved most beneficial for forecasting performance in epidemiological contexts where changes in transmission were highly consistent year-on-year.
We found the inclusion of this component had the greatest performance benefit for RSV, followed by influenza, with only marginal benefit found for SARS-CoV-2.
The patterns of RSV transmission are highly seasonal, with the timing of epidemic growth, peak and decline relatively consistent from one year to the next.
These stable dynamics were very well captured by our periodic Gaussian process, enabling accurate prediction of RSV case incidence.
While influenza epidemics typically recur at similar times year-to-year, the emergence of new viral strains can produce dynamics that are not well captured by the periodic Gaussian process.

This was evident in our application to the 2025 influenza season in Australia, where the unexpected emergence of the influenza A(H3N2) subclade K (Dapat et al. 2025) produced a prolonged period of heightened influenza case incidence.
text.formatted: This was evident in our application to the 2025 influenza season in Australia, where the unexpected emergence of the influenza A(H3N2) subclade K <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Dapat et al. 2025</ref>) produced a prolonged period of heightened influenza case incidence.

text.text: As our model does not capture strain or sub-type-level variation in growth (Davies et al. 2021; Eales et al. 2025), the model instead incorrectly predicted that case incidence would decline following the initial peak.
text.formatted: As our model does not capture strain or sub-type-level variation in growth <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Davies et al. 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Eales et al. 2025)</ref>, the model instead incorrectly predicted that case incidence would decline following the initial peak.

text.text: However, the emergence of subclade K was an unusual epidemiological event, and it is possible that the performance of our model in forecasting influenza would be greater in a more typical season.
This non-periodicity was most evident for SARS-CoV-2, where epidemics have not followed a stable seasonal pattern across the 2023-2025 years.

While these nonperiodic dynamics limited the model's ability to predict changes in growth rate ahead of time, our forecasts still proved capable of adapting to these changes once they were evident in the data.

Further, the inclusion of the periodic term is not necessarily harmful for overall performance in such non-periodic settings, as the magnitude of the term can automatically be shrunk towards zero during inference if periodicity is able to be ruled out.
Our estimates of the seasonal Gaussian process f seasonal should not be interpreted as equivalent to a seasonal forcing term on transmission.

Instead, this term likely captures a combined effect of changes in both the rate at which the virus can be transmitted (i.e. seasonal forcing, due to changes in human behaviour or viral trans-10 . missibility) and changes in population immunity (with reductions in transmission due to susceptible depletion and increases due to waning immunity).

To separate out these components, our model would need to be able to explicitly capture the effects of accumulating immunity (due to exposure) and depleting immunity (due to waning) on the population-scale transmission of respiratory viruses.
This remains a difficult task due to the complex dynamics of respiratory virus immunity and our poor understanding of the proportion of infections that are detected in case data.

Accurate forecasts of seasonal respiratory virus burden can aid public health decision-makers in critical areas such as medical workforce scheduling, testing and supply chain planning and public communications (Muscatello et al. 2017; Moss et al. 2018; Frounfelker et al. 2025; Christen et al. 2026).

text.text: A large number of respiratory virus forecasting programs are currently running (e.g. Gozzi et al. 2026; Hines et al. 2026; Henderson et al. 2026), and improving the performance of these forecasts is an active field of research.

text.text: Our results show that capturing the effects of school holidays and seasonal changes in transmission can substantially improve the performance of respiratory virus forecasts.

Such improvements may be of the greatest utility around peaks in epidemic activity, which in many settings (including ours), often coincide with the onset of school holidays (Cauchemez et al. 2008; Garza et al. 2013).
text.formatted: Such improvements may be of the greatest utility around peaks in epidemic activity, which in many settings (including ours), often coincide with the onset of school holidays <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Cauchemez et al. 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Garza et al. 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Our model is currently being used to produce real-time forecasts of RSV, influenza and SARS-CoV-2 across eight states and territories in Australia and in New Zealand on a weekly basis as part of the Australia-Aotearoa Winter Situational Assessment Program, with evaluation to follow.

Our results are likely to generalise to respiratory virus forecasting work in other settings, and the inclusion of holiday and seasonal effects should be considered where similar patterns in transmission and reporting can be identified.
We consider the log-transformed effective reproduction number log R(t ) to be made up of five additive components:

The functions ω S (t ) and ω P (t ) capture changes in transmission due to the school holidays and public holidays respectively (e.g. due to changes in contact behaviour), while f seasonal (t ) captures annually-periodic changes in the transmission rate and f noise (t ) captures any variation not explained by the other three terms.
The baseline c is included to capture any net difference from log R(t ) = 0 across the fitting period.
For the school holiday term ω S (t ), we estimate two separate effects.

The value ω between-term captures any changes to transmission across the shorter between-term school holidays, which are two weeks long and occur every (Southern Hemisphere) autumn, winter and spring, while ω summer captures transmission changes across the summer holidays, which are approximately six weeks long (and coincide with the Christmas and New Year holiday period in Australia).
These effects apply whenever time t is in the respective set of time-steps H between-term or H summer .
Otherwise, ω S (t ) is zero:

text.text: We estimate a separate effect of each named public holiday in a similar manner.

In the case where a public holiday fell on a weekend and was officially observed on the preceding Friday or following Monday, we assumed this could have a different effect on transmission and as such estimated a separate effect here (for example, we estimate one effect for 'New Year's Day' and one for 'New Year's Day (Observed)').

The term f seasonal (t ) captures any seasonal variation in R(t ) that recurs on a periodic, annual basis.
We capture this behaviour by modelling f seasonal (t ) as a Gaussian process with a periodic squared-exponential kernel: with ω0 = 2π/365.25 such that the period of the process is 365.25 days.
Finally, the term f noise (t ) captures any variation not more readily explained by the previous three terms.
We model this term as a Gaussian process with a Matérn 5/2 kernel: with this kernel selected to capture an intermediate level of smoothness in the noise process.

text.text: To improve the computational efficiency of model fitting given the long timeseries used in our model (multiple years of data), the Matérn and periodic Gaussian processes were approximated via Hilbert space Gaussian processes (HSGP) and linear low-rank approximations respectively following the approach presented in Riutort-Mayol et al. text.text: The two methods approximate a Gaussian process with a linear combination of K basis functions, reducing the computational complexity of inference with Gaussian process priors from O (n 3 ) to O (nK + K ), where n is the number of time-points evaluated and K is typically less than n.

text.text: To calculate skill scores, we produced a baseline model where case incidence follows a random-walk process, with 7-day seasonality imposed to capture any day-of-week effects (i.e. an ARIMA(0,0,0)(0,1,0) 7 model).
Naive forecasts were produced on the natural scale with a lower truncation applied at zero to prevent negative counts.

The magnitude of the random walk was informed by case incidence observations for each location-pathogen pair since January 1 2024, and constraints were applied so that projected incidence was non-negative.

Overall skill scores were then calculated as one minus the average CRPS for our forecasts divided by the average CRPS of the baseline forecasts across a given range X (defining our aggregation of forecast round, jurisdiction, pathogen, horizon):
For the sensitivity analyses, forecasts without certain components (e.g. the seasonal Gaussian process) were produced by constraining the value of those components to be zero.

text.text: In addition to the use of historically produced data for the rounds spanning from May 2025 through to December 2025, additional synthetic rounds were produced by truncating case incidence data.

A total of 12 rounds of RSV data were produced for Queensland and New South Wales starting from February 2025 to capture the early increases in case incidence observed in these jurisdictions (see Supplementary Figure 2) and four rounds of RSV, influenza and SARS-CoV-2 data for Victoria in April and May 2025 to capture the period of early epidemic growth and align coverage with other jurisdictions.
